overview: Emund the Old was Swedish king whose reign ended the older line before the rise of Stenkil. The profile is anchored by concrete turning points: c. 1000 — Approximate birth context; c. 1050 — Becomes king; 1050s — Ecclesiastical tensions.
He died in 1060, and his reign belongs to the wider story of Scandinavian state formation, Christianization, dynastic conflict, and northern Europe’s ties to England, the Baltic, and the Empire.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Emund the Old was Swedish king whose reign ended the older line before the rise of Stenkil. The profile is anchored by concrete turning points: c. 1000 — Approximate birth context; c. 1050 — Becomes king; 1050s — Ecclesiastical tensions.
He died in 1060, and his reign belongs to the wider story of Scandinavian state formation, Christianization, dynastic conflict, and northern Europe’s ties to England, the Baltic, and the Empire.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Emund the Old was born c. 1000. His family background is usually placed in House of Munsö / early Swedish line, though early Scandinavian genealogy can be uncertain and politically shaped.
Emund the Old's early life belonged to the medieval Scandinavian world, where kinship, sea routes, church contacts, assemblies, and armed followings shaped the opportunities available to a ruler.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Emund the Old is one of the more obscure Swedish kings, and his character is barely recoverable. Adam of Bremen, the main source, regarded him with suspicion, presenting him as lukewarm or unreliable in matters of the church and critical of his dealings with the archbishopric of Hamburg-Bremen — a hostile view from a writer deeply invested in that church's authority over the north.

He is remembered for a disputed boundary settlement with Denmark and for the contested succession that followed his death, after which the old royal line gave way to a new dynasty. The negative tinge in the record reflects Adam's ecclesiastical priorities more than a rounded judgement of the man.

The honest assessment is that Emund survives as a name at the end of a dynasty, seen mainly through the disapproval of a churchman who distrusted his independence from Hamburg-Bremen. His personality cannot be reconstructed with any confidence from so partial and unfriendly a record.

contentSections.title: As king of Sweden
paragraphs: Emund the Old ruled in a poorly documented period. His reign is associated with ecclesiastical tensions and the transition from the older royal line to the House of Stenkil.
As King of Sweden, Emund the Old had to turn dynastic claim into workable authority through alliances, military pressure, church support, and acceptance by regional elites.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Died around 1060; Stenkil succeeded him as Swedish kingship remained contested between dynastic and regional interests.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: His legacy lies in a dynastic transition more than in a richly recorded personal reign.
Later saga, saintly, or national traditions often amplified Emund the Old's reputation, so the article separates near-contemporary evidence from later memory where possible.
